video_title: Lawfare Daily:  Escalate to What End? Trump's Plan for the Iran War After the Midterms
gist: Former NSC Iran directors Cole Bunzel, Nate Swanson and Ari Tabatabai assess whether Trump escalates the eight-month Iran war after the midterms, with crude near $105, Gulf energy exposed, US munitions short, and Iran running out the clock; base case is a grinding standoff with flare-ups.

insights.claim: Energy prices and pump prices pushed Trump to the June memorandum of understanding with Iran, which was more favorable to Iran than the status quo ante; with the midterms past, he no longer needs low gas prices, so the gloves could come off after November 3.
insights.speaker: Cole Bunzel
insights.so_what: A post-midterm escalation window raises oil and Gulf-energy tail risk from November.

insights.claim: Ari Tabatabai sees a 'danger zone' between the midterms and the new Congress in January, when a lame-duck Trump may escalate to force a deal before oversight, appropriations fights and impeachment efforts begin.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Timing of potential strikes clusters in November-December, relevant for oil and defense positioning.

insights.claim: Crude was at about $105 a barrel the prior week, with the war in its eighth month; both sides believe time favors them and the panel says neither is right because both are losing.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Oil is already elevated at about $105, so further escalation starts from a stressed price base.

insights.claim: The panel's consensus lightning-round forecast for New Year's Day is the same endless grinding standoff, with another round of strikes ('Epic Fury light') in late November.
insights.speaker: Cole Bunzel
insights.so_what: Base case is periodic flare-ups rather than resolution or full-scale war, implying a persistent risk premium in energy.

insights.claim: A worst-case post-midterm scenario has US strikes on Iranian civilian infrastructure (water, electricity) triggering Iranian tit-for-tat hits on Gulf water, power and energy sites, which are more vulnerable than Iran's, and Trump has largely held back so far partly because the Gulf has quietly urged restraint.
insights.speaker: Cole Bunzel
insights.so_what: Damage to Gulf energy capacity would extend supply disruption beyond tanker flows through Hormuz.

insights.claim: Damaged Gulf production and export infrastructure would add rebuild costs and a long tail to global energy supply, beyond the acute Strait of Hormuz tanker-flow problem.
insights.speaker: Cole Bunzel
insights.so_what: Price effects could persist after any ceasefire because capacity, not just shipping, is impaired.

insights.claim: The UAE and Saudi economic model of an 'oasis of stability' is threatened beyond energy, including data storage and trade, and the IRGC has explicitly threatened undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz and information storage.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Gulf data-center, financial-hub and subsea-cable exposure is a non-obvious risk channel for tech and infrastructure investors.

insights.claim: A Reuters report said the UAE struck its own quiet deal to unfreeze Iranian assets in return for not being struck since May, echoing 2019-2020 when the Emirates became the primary sanctions-evasion mechanism for Iran.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Gulf hedging with Iran reduces US leverage and may erode US basing influence.

insights.claim: Iran's Houthi partners struck Saudi Arabia this month, killing an American at Riyadh airport and hitting oil fields, but the Houthis act with their own agency; their disruption of a second chokepoint helps Iran pressure the US and Gulf toward ending the conflict.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Red Sea and Saudi risk is not fully controlled by Tehran, making escalation harder to forecast.

insights.claim: US interceptor and key munitions shortages are felt across combatant commands, with EUCOM and PACOM complaining about needs for Taiwan, Korea and Ukraine contingencies, and the administration claims it needs $22 billion to replace munitions.
insights.speaker: Cole Bunzel
insights.so_what: Sustained demand for interceptors and munitions supports defense-procurement budgets and supply-chain expansion.

insights.claim: Counterintuitively, munitions shortages can argue for escalation in White House logic: one decisive push to end the war would free supply chains for other commands.
insights.speaker: Cole Bunzel
insights.so_what: Shortages do not necessarily restrain US action and may accelerate a short, intense strike package ('Epic Fury 2.0').

insights.claim: The US is in a 'mowing the lawn' scenario with no political objective, because it planned for regime fracture and had no plan B beyond repeated strikes on radar and missile sites, so it keeps depleting stockpiles.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: A strategy with no endpoint implies open-ended defense spending and no resolution catalyst.

insights.claim: A special-forces raid to seize buried enriched uranium is seen less as a credible nonproliferation step than as a made-for-TV spectacle letting Trump claim victory and change the narrative.
insights.speaker: Cole Bunzel
insights.so_what: A headline-grabbing operation could be a short-term volatility event without changing the underlying standoff.

insights.claim: Iran is running down the clock because it believes its elite is consolidating around the IRGC while the US government fractures, and that the worst has passed after decapitation strikes and nuclear damage, with no US appetite for ground troops.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Low odds Iran concedes after the midterms undermines the market assumption that escalation leads quickly to a deal.

insights.claim: Iran has no IAEA oversight, so a covert nuclear breakout attempt cannot be ruled out, and its likelihood rises the longer the conflict becomes a forever war.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Nuclear breakout remains a fat-tail risk for geopolitical risk premia.

insights.claim: Iran sees this war as connected to the Soleimani strike, the 12-day war and February, so it fears the US and Israel will return after any ceasefire and is likely to keep pushing while the US is low on munitions.
insights.speaker: Cole Bunzel
insights.so_what: Iran is unlikely to accept an off-ramp that lets the US regroup, so a durable ceasefire is hard to price.

insights.claim: The June MOU is a poor deal for the US but the least-bad option, and Iran doubts US credibility to honor any deal, since Epic Fury started in the middle of negotiations.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Diplomatic resets are fragile; the June ceasefire lasted three weeks.

insights.claim: A best case is a Gulf-led version of the MOU in which the Gulf bails out Trump and Iran, letting Trump avoid owning a deal his base sees as a loser.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Gulf mediation is the plausible de-escalation path to watch.

insights.claim: Trump's Iran decisions bypass the NSC interagency process, are made within a tiny inner circle, and even insiders who doubted the war did not speak up, increasing the odds of abrupt reversals.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Policy whiplash means headline risk for oil and defense names is hard to forecast from process.

insights.claim: Congress can pressure war funding via the budget, but cutting interceptor funding is politically costly and appropriations are hard to silo, so the panel expects the president to blame Democrats rather than accept real restrictions.
insights.speaker: Ari Tabatabai
insights.so_what: Defense budget fights, including a $1.5 trillion DoD request, will be a focal point in 2027.
